ideas.hypothesis: Sacrifice ratios computed with trimmed-mean or weighted-median core measures are higher and more stable across episodes than those computed with headline CPI, because core measures strip supply shocks that falsely lower apparent costs.

sources.role: finding: different sacrifice ratios for headline vs core in EA and US
measure: alternative core inflation indices
method: trimmed means and bootstrap optimal trimming

ideas.test: Ball-style disinflation episode analysis for OECD countries 1970-2019 computed with headline, ex-food-energy, trimmed mean, weighted median; compare means and variance of ratios across episodes.
ideas.disconfirming: Sacrifice ratios do not differ or are less stable with core measures.

ideas.hypothesis: Sacrifice ratios are lower in periods when the NKPC is in a forward-looking regime than in a backward-looking regime, as identified by Markov switching.

sources.role: method: Markov-switching NKPC regimes
finding: stable sacrifice ratio despite regime change in Canada
method: output-inflation trade-off tests with residual diagnostics

ideas.test: Estimate Markov-switching hybrid NKPC on quarterly data for 5-10 countries 1970-2019; compute sacrifice ratio within each regime's disinflation episodes.
ideas.disconfirming: Sacrifice ratios are equal across regimes, or higher in forward-looking regimes.

ideas.hypothesis: Greater central bank transparency/credibility raises the weight on forward-looking expectations in the hybrid NKPC and flattens the backward-looking component.

method: output-inflation trade-off tests
mechanism: open-economy NK Phillips curves

ideas.test: Panel of 20-30 countries 1990-2019: GMM hybrid NKPC with forward weight interacted with Dincer-Eichengreen transparency index.
ideas.disconfirming: Forward-looking weight does not rise with transparency.

ideas.hypothesis: Since the mid-2000s, headline inflation has become more attracted to core than vice versa; central banks that respond to core rather than headline achieve lower inflation volatility.

sources.role: finding: changed headline-core relationship and survey forecasts
finding: reduced cyclical sensitivity of inflation
measure: market-based inflation expectations
setting: price stability as objective

ideas.test: Bivariate VAR/ECM attractor tests of headline and core for 15 countries in two subperiods; then compare inflation volatility by whether reaction functions load on core.
ideas.disconfirming: Core is not an attractor for headline in the later period.

ideas.hypothesis: The output-gap slope of the Phillips curve is steeper for core than for headline inflation, so the inflation-output trade-off is better measured with core.

finding: core and headline dynamics differ

ideas.test: Estimate Phillips curves with headline and core inflation for US, EA, Canada 1985-2019; compare slope coefficients and stability.
ideas.disconfirming: Slopes are similar or steeper for headline.

ideas.hypothesis: Headline-based sacrifice ratios fall during periods of energy-price volatility, because supply shocks blur the trade-off; controlling for oil shocks restores comparability with core-based ratios.

ideas.test: Rolling-window Phillips curve estimates for US and EA 1980-2019 with and without oil price controls.
ideas.disconfirming: Headline trade-off unaffected by energy volatility.
